subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Over and Under: Weaving a Paper Mat
periods.textbook_anchor: Patterns with Threads — Students weave blue and yellow paper strips over and under to create a mat (p. 133)
materials: magnifying glass or mobile phone camera (one per group)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of a baya weaver bird nest (p. 133)

time_bands.activity: Open with a brief look at Textbook p. 133 — students study the image of the baya weaver bird's nest and share what they notice about how the grass strips are arranged. The teacher asks: 'How do you think the bird manages to hold all those strips together without any glue?' Students turn and talk in pairs.

The teacher explains the over-and-under principle on the board using two drawn lines, then points back to Textbook p. 133 to show how the same pattern appears in cloth, mats, and baskets woven from coconut fibre, bamboo, jute, and other natural materials around us.

Students tape their blue strips vertically to the desk, then weave yellow strips through — over, under, over, under — pressing each new strip snugly against the last. When the mat is complete, they hold a portion of any fabric they are wearing under a magnifying glass or zoom in with a phone camera to spot the same criss-cross pattern described in Textbook p. 134.

Whole-class share-out: pairs describe one similarity they spotted between their woven mat and the fabric weave. The teacher draws out mentions of natural woven objects students have seen at home — cane baskets, grass mats, palm-leaf baskets — connecting the weaving principle to familiar everyday objects.

periods.implied_lo: Students can demonstrate the over-and-under interlacing principle used to construct woven structures.
periods.section_context: Baya weaver bird nest, over-and-under weaving technique, blue and yellow paper strips as warp and weft, woven mat, magnifying-glass observation of cloth weave, natural woven materials (coconut fibre, palm reeds, bamboo, grass, jute, cotton, silk), Indian muslin.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether anyone's family uses woven baskets, mats, or winnowing fans at home, and gently draw out the variety of natural materials their families use — this surfaces the knowledge that different regions weave different plants without the teacher naming the regions first.

periods.textbook_anchor: Traditions of Weaving — Students discuss regional handloom traditions of India (p. 133)
materials: India outline map printed or drawn on the board
periods.visual_aids: Board sketch of India with four regions marked: Tamil Nadu, Kashmir, Odisha, Gujarat

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the Traditions of Weaving section and pauses after each named tradition — Kanjeevaram, Pashmina, Ikat — asking students to repeat the name and guess what the fabric might feel like. Students look at the textbook images and describe colours and patterns they notice.

Students discuss in small groups: 'India has been weaving for over 4,000 years — what might that tell us about how important cloth is to people's lives?' Groups then share one idea each. The teacher notes key phrases on the board: livelihood, heritage, handmade, community. The contrast between handloom and textile-mill production is introduced through a pair of questions: 'What might be different about cloth woven by one person's hands compared with cloth made by a fast machine?'

The teacher marks Tamil Nadu, Kashmir, Odisha, and Gujarat on the board map and students call out the matching tradition for each region, using the textbook for support. A short discussion follows on why weaving traditions vary by region — available plants, climate, community practices — drawing on what students know from their own surroundings.

Each student writes one sentence in their notebook: 'A handloom tradition I found interesting is ___ because ___.' Two or three students share aloud. The teacher closes by noting that over 45 lakh people — especially women and rural artisans — depend on handloom work for their livelihood.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe how regional natural and cultural conditions shape distinct handcraft traditions.
periods.section_context: Handloom fabric, hand-operated loom, Kanjeevaram (Tamil Nadu), Pashmina (Kashmir), Ikat (Odisha and Gujarat), 45 lakh weavers, textile mills, weaving as livelihood and heritage.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If any student's family has a connection to handloom weaving, tailoring, or selling cloth, invite them to share briefly — this personalises the livelihood dimension without requiring preparation and honours knowledge students bring from home.

periods.activity_title: Spinning a Thread: From Cotton Ball to Strand
periods.textbook_anchor: Thread — Students pull and twist cotton fibres around a pencil to make a thread strand (p. 135)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 135 and the teacher introduces the idea that every thread begins as a fibre — an individual fine strand. Students gently pull at their cotton ball and describe in one word how it feels. The teacher asks: 'What do you think happens if you twist these loose fibres together?'

Students follow the steps in Textbook p. 135: pull the cotton into a loose strand, twist it slowly with their fingers and feel it grow stronger, then wind the strand onto a pencil — twisting as they go, adding more cotton — to build a longer thread. Students repeat the wind-and-twist cycle until they have a visible thread length and notice how twisting locks the fibres together.

The teacher introduces the charkha and explains Gandhi ji's promotion of hand-spinning as a symbol of self-sufficiency, connecting the students' just-completed hand-twist to the larger movement. A brief discussion follows: 'Why might spinning your own thread matter to a community that wants to be independent?'

Students draw and label a simple two-step diagram in their notebooks: (1) loose fibres → (2) twisted thread, and write one sentence about what spinning does to the fibres. Two or three students share their sentences aloud before the activity closes.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how twisting individual fibres together produces a stronger thread.
periods.section_context: Raw cotton fibres, twisting and spinning process, pencil as spindle, charkha, khadi, Gandhi ji and self-sufficiency, fibres (individual fine strands).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether anyone has seen a charkha at home, in a photograph, or at a local fair — students who have can describe it and the teacher can connect it to the hand-twist they just did, making the technology feel continuous rather than historical.

periods.activity_title: Natural or Synthetic? Sorting the Fibres Around Us
periods.textbook_anchor: Thread — Students examine everyday clothes and objects and classify their fibres as natural or synthetic in a table (p. 138)
materials: assorted small fabric scraps or everyday objects with visible fabric (bags, scarves, socks — one set per group of three)
periods.visual_aids: Board two-column table: Natural Fibres | Synthetic Fibres

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a two-column table on the board (Natural Fibres | Synthetic Fibres) and asks students to call out any fibre names they know. After populating the board table with student contributions, the teacher introduces the distinction from Textbook p. 138: bamboo, cotton, linen, wool, silk are natural; rayon, nylon, polyester, terylene are synthetic.

Groups of three examine their fabric scraps and everyday objects, then open Textbook p. 138 and complete the observation table — recording each item, its likely fibre (using the textbook and any labels present), whether natural or synthetic, and one thing they like or notice about it. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'How did this fibre get from a plant or animal to a thread?'

Groups share their most surprising finding — an object they assumed was natural that turned out to be synthetic, or vice versa. The teacher adds the silk moth's life cycle (eggs → caterpillar → cocoon → moth) to the board, explaining that silk — one of the finest natural fibres — begins as a caterpillar's cocoon, connecting the life-science strand to the observation task just completed.
Students write one complete sentence in their notebooks describing one natural fibre and its source: 'Silk comes from ___.' Brief share-out closes the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify materials as natural or synthetic fibres and identify the plant or animal source of natural fibres.
periods.section_context: Natural fibres (bamboo, cotton, linen, wool, silk) and synthetic fibres (rayon, nylon, polyester, terylene), silk moth life cycle (eggs, caterpillar, cocoon, moth), everyday clothes and bags examined for fibre type, observation table.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Encourage students to check the care labels inside the fabric scraps — many carry fibre content — turning reading a label into a real-world classification skill and prompting the question of why manufacturers name the fibre.

periods.activity_title: Nature's Stitcher: Leaf-Plate and First Running Stitch
periods.textbook_anchor: Crafting with Needle and Thread — Students pin broad leaves or paper together with toothpick-twigs to make a plate or spoon (p. 139)
materials: broad leaves (palash, teak, or jackfruit) or A4 paper pieces cut to leaf size (one set per group of four)
pre-threaded needles (blunt, one per student — teacher threads beforehand)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of the tailorbird stitching leaves (p. 139)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 139 and examine the tailorbird image. The teacher asks: 'The tailorbird has no needle — what does it use instead, and what does it use as thread?' Students share observations, and the teacher draws the parallel between the bird's plant-fibre or spider-silk stitching and the toothpicks and leaves students are about to use.

In groups of four, students collect and stack two or three broad leaves (or paper substitutes) and use toothpicks to pin them together along the edges to create a simple leaf plate or spoon, following the idea in Textbook p. 139. They observe how the toothpick-pins hold the layers and discuss how this resembles stitching — a pointed tool piercing material to hold pieces together.

Each student picks up a pre-threaded blunt needle and two small cloth scraps. Following the running-stitch steps described in Textbook p. 140, students bring the needle up at one point, push it down, bring it up again — up, down, up, down — in a straight line. The teacher circulates and checks that the knot at the thread end is holding and that each student completes at least one full row of stitches.

Students hold their stitched cloth pieces up and the teacher asks: 'If one stitch came undone, what might happen to the whole row?' A brief whole-class reflection connects the running stitch to its practical uses — mending a tear, sewing a button — closing on the life-skill dimension of the activity.

periods.implied_lo: Students can demonstrate a basic joining technique — using a pointed tool and a flexible strand — to connect two separate pieces of material.
periods.section_context: Tailorbird nest-stitching with plant fibres and spider silk, broad leaves (palash, teak, jackfruit) and toothpicks as stitching analogue, blunt needle and thread, running stitch (up-down-up-down in a straight line), cloth scraps, mending tears and sewing buttons.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether anyone has watched a family member mend clothing or stitch at home — invite them to describe the motion they saw, which helps the class connect the school activity to everyday domestic skill without requiring any materials from home.

periods.activity_title: Patchwork Together: Joining Cloth into a Usable Piece
periods.textbook_anchor: Crafting with Needle and Thread — Students use running stitch to join multiple cloth pieces into a table cloth, mat, or coaster (p. 140)
materials: cloth scraps of varying colours (4–6 per student — collected from tailor shops or old cloth)

time_bands.activity: The teacher distributes cloth scraps and reminds students of the running stitch they have already practised. Students briefly plan — by laying scraps flat and overlapping edges — what shape or object they will create: a small coaster, mat, or cleaning cloth, as suggested in Textbook p. 140.

Students stitch scraps together piece by piece using the running stitch, overlapping edges slightly before stitching. As they work, they choose the order and colour arrangement of their pieces. The teacher encourages students to think about patterns — alternating colours, repeating shapes — connecting the visual rhythm to the weave patterns explored earlier in the chapter.

Students give their finished piece a name and one-line description: what it is, what it could be used for. They place the pieces on their desks for a brief gallery walk around the room, noticing the variety of colour arrangements and sizes their classmates produced.

The teacher closes with the question: 'If you needed more cloth scraps, where could you get them without buying new cloth?' — prompting students to think about tailors' offcuts, old garments, and the idea of resourcefulness, setting the stage for the recycling theme ahead.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use a simple joining stitch to combine multiple pieces of material into a functional, composed object.
periods.section_context: Cloth scraps from tailor shops or old cloth, running stitch to join multiple pieces, patchwork table cloth, mat, coaster, cleaning cloth, colour and pattern arrangement.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Circulate and ask each student what they chose to make and why — this brief conversation surfaces creative decision-making and allows the teacher to note students who are struggling with the stitch so they can be quietly paired with a more confident neighbour.

periods.textbook_anchor: Stitch and Decorate — Students explore regional embroidery traditions of India (p. 141)
materials: India outline map drawn on the board
periods.visual_aids: Board outline map of India with states marked for each embroidery tradition

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 141 and reads through the regional embroidery names — Chikankari, Banjara, Kantha, Gota, Phulkari, Toda, Kashmiri, Khneng — asking students to repeat each name aloud. Students look at the textbook images and share what colours, shapes, or feelings they notice in each style.

Students work in pairs to match each embroidery style to its region using the textbook, then call out answers as the teacher plots each tradition on the board map with a coloured label. Discussion questions: 'Why might embroidery patterns from Punjab look different from those in Meghalaya? What local materials or stories might each community be stitching into the cloth?'

Pairs discuss: 'Stitching is not just about joining cloth — what else does it do for the people who make it and the people who wear it?' Groups share ideas (identity, storytelling, livelihood, beauty, ceremony). The teacher adds Bandhani tie-dye and Kala cotton from Gujarat as further examples of textile art that carries cultural meaning.

Each student writes two sentences in their notebook: one naming a regional embroidery tradition and where it comes from, and one explaining what that tradition tells us about the community that created it. Two or three students share aloud to close.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect specific regional craft traditions to their cultural and geographical contexts.
periods.section_context: Regional embroidery traditions: Chikankari (Lucknow), Banjara (Rajasthan), Kantha (West Bengal, Odisha, Tripura), Gota (Rajasthan), Phulkari (Punjab), Toda (Tamil Nadu), Kashmiri embroidery, Khneng (Meghalaya), Bandhani tie-dye (Rajasthan), Kala cotton (Gujarat).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students if they own or have seen clothing with embroidery, mirror work, or printed patterns at home or during festivals — this grounds the global-map discussion in personal experience and may surface traditions from the students' own regions not listed in the textbook.

periods.activity_title: Give Cloth a Second Life: Recycling and Reflecting
periods.textbook_anchor: Recycle — Students discuss why old clothes should not be thrown away and explore cultural practices of repurposing cloth (p. 143)
materials: 3–5 pieces of fabric scrap (any size — collected beforehand by the teacher)

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a worn piece of scrap cloth and asks: 'What should happen to this?' Students respond freely. The teacher then opens Textbook p. 143 and reads the Recycle section aloud, pausing at hand-me-downs, repurposed cloth, and quilts made from joined scraps. Students name anything at home that was once clothing and became something else.

Students discuss in small groups: 'We should not throw old clothes away — why?' (Textbook p. 143 reflection task). Groups share reasons; the teacher writes key ideas on the board — resource use, environment, family tradition, livelihood for rag-pickers and recyclers — and connects them to the cultural practice of quilt-making from cloth scraps as an embedded Indian tradition rather than a modern trend.

Individual reflection and writing: students respond to the two Textbook p. 143 reflection questions in their notebooks — (1) Have you ever reused or recycled a piece of cloth? What was made from it? and (2) If one thread breaks in a woven mat, what might happen? Why is each thread important? Students who finish write one more sentence about a cloth-recycling practice they know from their family or neighbourhood.

A few students share their thread-breaking reflection, and the teacher draws the metaphor gently outward — one broken thread weakens the whole, just as one person's choice to reuse cloth or buy handloom cloth connects to the livelihood of many weavers. Students close by writing one personal commitment in their notebook: one way they will treat cloth more carefully from now on.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate reasons for reusing and repurposing cloth and connect personal behaviour to its broader social and environmental consequences.
periods.section_context: Old clothes and hand-me-downs, repurposing cloth into other items, quilt-making from cloth scraps, reasons not to discard old clothes (resource use, environment, tradition), thread-breaking consequence in woven mat, personal recycling commitment.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students what their grandparents or older relatives do with clothes that are too worn to wear — stories of razais (quilts) made from old saris or dupattas are common across many Indian homes and make the cultural tradition vivid and immediate.

assessment_items.question_text: A baya weaver bird builds its nest by passing grass strips over and then under other strips, again and again. Which of the following objects is made using the same over-and-under principle?

options.label: A
options.text: A clay pot shaped on a wheel

options.label: B
options.text: A cane basket woven from bamboo strips

options.label: C
options.text: A glass bottle blown from molten sand

options.label: D
options.text: A metal spoon cast in a mould

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item checks whether students transfer the over-and-under interlacing principle from the weaving activity to a new object. A clay pot, glass bottle, and metal spoon are all formed by different shaping processes (moulding, blowing, casting) that do not use interlacing.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can demonstrate the over-and-under interlacing principle used to construct woven structures.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'clay pot' suggests the student associates any handmade object with weaving, without recognising that pot-making uses a moulding and shaping process rather than interlacing strips.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'glass bottle' suggests the student has not distinguished between craft processes — glass-blowing uses heat and air, not interlacing.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'metal spoon' suggests the student is thinking broadly about making objects but has not connected the specific over-and-under mechanism to the correct material form.

assessment_items.question_text: India has many different handloom traditions. Name any two regional handloom traditions of India and write the region or state each one comes from.
expected_elements: Names at least two distinct regional handloom traditions (e.g., Kanjeevaram, Pashmina, Ikat).
Correctly links each named tradition to its region or state (e.g., Kanjeevaram — Tamil Nadu; Pashmina — Kashmir; Ikat — Odisha or Gujarat).
Uses the textbook terms or close equivalents — no invented names accepted.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two correctly matched pairs from: Kanjeevaram–Tamil Nadu, Pashmina–Kashmir, Ikat–Odisha, Ikat–Gujarat. Partial credit if the tradition is named but the region is missing or reversed. Do not penalise spelling variations in the tradition names.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe how regional natural and cultural conditions shape distinct handcraft traditions.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

expected_elements: Names at least two distinct regional handloom traditions (e.g., Kanjeevaram, Pashmina, Ikat).
Correctly links each named tradition to its region or state (e.g., Kanjeevaram — Tamil Nadu; Pashmina — Kashmir; Ikat — Odisha or Gujarat).
Uses the textbook terms or close equivalents — no invented names accepted.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya pulls apart a ball of raw cotton and tries to lift one loose fibre. It breaks easily. Then she twists several fibres together slowly and tries to pull the twisted strand apart. What is the most likely result, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The twisted strand breaks just as easily, because the fibres are still the same material.

options.label: B
options.text: The twisted strand is stronger, because twisting locks the fibres together so they pull against each other instead of separating.

options.label: C
options.text: The twisted strand becomes waterproof, because twisting removes the air from between the fibres.

options.label: D
options.text: The twisted strand is weaker, because twisting stretches and thins the individual fibres.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item targets the mechanical explanation of spinning — that twisting creates friction and interlocking between fibres, increasing tensile strength. A tests a common misconception that material properties are fixed regardless of arrangement. C introduces an unrelated property (waterproofing). D reverses the actual effect.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how twisting individual fibres together produces a stronger thread.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option shows the student has not grasped that structure affects strength — they believe material identity alone determines properties.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option shows a confusion between structural change and a chemical or physical property change (waterproofing), indicating incomplete understanding of what spinning does.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has reversed the cause-and-effect relationship, possibly confusing stretching with strengthening.

assessment_items.question_text:
Look at the list of fibres below. Sort them into two groups — Natural and Synthetic — and for each natural fibre, write ONE plant or animal it comes from.

Fibres: Cotton, Nylon, Silk, Polyester, Wool
expected_elements: Cotton correctly placed in the Natural group, with source: cotton plant.
Silk correctly placed in the Natural group, with source: silkworm (or silk moth caterpillar).
Wool correctly placed in the Natural group, with source: sheep (or another wool-bearing animal).
Nylon correctly placed in the Synthetic group.
Polyester correctly placed in the Synthetic group.
assessment_items.annotation: All five fibres must be correctly classified for full marks. Partial credit for three or four correct placements. For natural fibres, accept any reasonable source (e.g., 'sheep' or 'lamb' for wool; 'caterpillar' or 'cocoon' or 'silkworm' for silk). Deduct if a synthetic fibre is given a plant/animal source.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify materials as natural or synthetic fibres and identify the plant or animal source of natural fibres.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: Cotton correctly placed in the Natural group, with source: cotton plant.
Silk correctly placed in the Natural group, with source: silkworm (or silk moth caterpillar).
Wool correctly placed in the Natural group, with source: sheep (or another wool-bearing animal).
Nylon correctly placed in the Synthetic group.
Polyester correctly placed in the Synthetic group.

assessment_items.question_text: The tailorbird sews leaves together to make a nest without using a needle. Which feature of the tailorbird's beak makes it able to do the same job as a needle?

options.label: A
options.text: It is long and curved, which helps the bird scoop fish from water.

options.label: B
options.text: It is sharp and pointed, which lets the bird pierce the leaf to push plant fibre through.

options.label: C
options.text: It is wide and flat, which lets the bird press the leaves firmly together.

options.label: D
options.text: It is hooked at the tip, which lets the bird tear the leaf into strips for weaving.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. The item tests whether students understood the functional parallel between the tailorbird's pointed beak and a sewing needle — both work by piercing the material. A confuses the tailorbird with a fish-eating bird. C describes a pressing rather than piercing action. D conflates stitching with weaving/tearing.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can demonstrate a basic joining technique — using a pointed tool and a flexible strand — to connect two separate pieces of material.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option suggests the student has confused the tailorbird with a water-hunting bird, indicating inattention to the bird's specific stitching behaviour described in the section.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option shows the student understands that joining is the goal but has confused the mechanism — pressing together versus piercing through.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has conflated stitching with weaving/tearing, confusing two different joining methods presented in the chapter.

assessment_items.task: You have stitched cloth scraps together into a patchwork piece. Now, imagine you are setting up a small display of your patchwork in the classroom. Write a short label (3–5 sentences) for your piece that explains: (1) what it is and what it could be used for, (2) how you made it — the type of stitch you used, and (3) one choice you made about the colours or pattern arrangement, and why.
assessment_items.scaffold: My patchwork piece is a ___ and can be used for ___. I made it by using a ___ stitch to join ___ pieces of cloth. I arranged the colours / pattern by ___ because ___.
format_of_output: May be accompanied by a quick sketch of the piece if the student wishes
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the label on completeness (all three points addressed), accuracy (running stitch named correctly), and the quality of the creative reasoning given for colour or pattern choice. A sketch is optional and not assessed separately. No single correct answer — accept any coherent design rationale.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use a simple joining stitch to combine multiple pieces of material into a functional, composed object.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can describe a self-made functional object, name the technique used to construct it, and give a reason for a creative design choice — showing that making and explaining are connected.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold gives three sentence starters. A strong response fills all three with specific, accurate detail. A weak response completes only one or two starters or uses vague language ('I made it nicely').
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names the object and a concrete use ('a small coaster for a cup'), correctly names 'running stitch', and gives a genuine reason for pattern choice ('I alternated red and blue so it would look like a pattern'). Weak: says 'I stitched cloth' with no further detail, or cannot name the stitch type.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who had difficulty stitching may describe what they attempted and what they would do differently. Students with fine-motor challenges may dictate the label to a peer or the teacher. A sketch alone (with no words) is insufficient but may supplement.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A display label is an authentic, real-world format that connects the making activity to the idea of sharing and communicating craft knowledge — matching the Exhibition task suggested in the Stitch and Decorate section.

assessment_items.question_text:
India has many regional embroidery traditions. Choose any ONE tradition from the list below and write: (a) the state or region it comes from, and (b) one thing that makes it special or different from other embroidery styles.

Traditions: Phulkari, Kantha, Chikankari, Toda
expected_elements: Correctly names the state or region for the chosen tradition (Phulkari–Punjab; Kantha–West Bengal/Odisha/Tripura; Chikankari–Lucknow/Uttar Pradesh; Toda–Tamil Nadu).

Gives at least one specific distinguishing feature of that tradition (e.g., Phulkari uses bright flower-like patterns; Kantha uses running stitch to create layered quilts; Chikankari is delicate white embroidery on fine fabric; Toda uses geometric patterns in black and red).
Response is in complete sentences or clearly organised points.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept region-level answers (e.g., 'eastern India' for Kantha) if the specific states were not memorised. For part (b), accept any reasonable distinguishing feature drawn from the textbook or from the classroom discussion — do not require an exact textbook phrase. Note: students from Punjab, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, or Tamil Nadu may provide richer detail from personal experience; this is desirable and should be acknowledged.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect specific regional craft traditions to their cultural and geographical contexts.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

assessment_items.question_text: Your neighbour wants to throw away a pile of old clothes that no longer fit anyone in the family. Write a short paragraph (4–6 sentences) to persuade them NOT to throw the clothes away. Give at least two specific reasons and suggest at least one thing they could do with the old clothes instead.
look_for: States at least two distinct reasons for not discarding old clothes (e.g., wasting resources, harming the environment, losing material that can be reused, taking away livelihood opportunities for rag-pickers or recyclers).
Suggests at least one concrete alternative use (e.g., pass to a younger sibling, donate, cut into cleaning cloths, stitch into a quilt).
Connects the personal choice to a consequence beyond the individual family (community, environment, or tradition).
Writing is persuasive in tone — not simply a list, but addressed to the neighbour.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an open-ended persuasive task. Assess on quality of reasoning (are the reasons specific and connected to the chapter content?) and persuasive tone (does the student address the neighbour rather than list facts?). Suggestions for alternative use should be practical and drawn from the chapter or from common experience. Regional variation in practice (e.g., making razais or floor mats from old saris) is acceptable and commendable. Do not penalise students whose suggestions reflect their own cultural practice.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate reasons for reusing and repurposing cloth and connect personal behaviour to its broader social and environmental consequences.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)
